confirmed.quote: the legal chess moves are exactly the moves of the model, nobody is in check, and the side to move has a legal move
confirmed.problem: (V1) as worded contradicts itself and the proof. The model never moves kings, but moves in Z are legal chess moves (they are the decisive events that (V3) punishes), so the legal chess moves cannot be exactly the model's moves. If they were, a side with no pawn move would have no legal move, contradicting the last clause. The proof sketch's step 'by (V1) the side to move always has a model move' then does not follow.
confirmed.fix: Replace (V1) by: 'the legal chess moves outside Z are exactly the pawn moves of the model, with the same resulting positions (en passant included), no such move gives check, nobody is in check, and the side to move has a legal move (a move in Z counts)'. In the proof replace 'by (V1) the side to move always has a model move, so play ends at a decisive event' with 'by (V1) the side to move always has a legal move, a pawn move or a move in Z; the pawn game is finite, so some decisive event occurs'.

verdict.reason: The wording of (V1) at 04_kings.tex:57 is inconsistent with the model's definition and with the proof. 02_rules.tex:33 says the model "never moves" the kings, and a move in Z is by definition a decisive event that (V3) punishes. Chess king moves in Z are therefore legal chess moves, so the legal chess moves cannot be exactly the model's moves. Read literally, (V1) rules out the very moves (V3) is about. The last clause, "the side to move has a legal move", is then also hard to read: with only model moves, a side with no pawn move has none. The proof's step "by (V1) the side to move always has a model move" does not follow from the stated text. The theorem is a [S] result, so the hypotheses should be stated exactly. The conclusion survives in substance, because the pawn game is finite and play must reach a decisive event. This is a statement-precision defect, not a false theorem, but a referee would raise it and the author should fix it.
verdict.better_fix: Replace (V1) with: "the legal chess moves outside Z are exactly the pawn moves of the model, with the same resulting positions (en passant included), no such move gives check, nobody is in check, and the side to move has a legal move (a move in Z counts)". In the proof, replace "by (V1) the side to move always has a model move, so play ends at a decisive event" with "by (V1) the side to move always has a legal move, a pawn move or a move in Z; the pawn game is finite, so some decisive event occurs". Also adjust the remark "a stalemate trap leaves the loser without a move (V1)" so it fits the new wording; it still fits, since the trap leaves no legal move at all.

The inference 'so (V3) holds' is therefore invalid, and the next paragraph refutes it: Kb4-c5 has a certificate of horizon 1 yet the chess result is a draw. confirmed.fix: Replace the second half of the sentence by: 'so (V3) holds in the promotion game wherever every move in Z has one. For chess, (V3) additionally needs the per-position check that a won promotion race is a won game; no margin on h replaces it (next paragraph).' Alternatively state (V3) and (V2) of Theorem 4.1 for the promotion game plus an explicit hypothesis that the promotion game and chess have the same result.

verdict.reason: The sentence in Theorem 4.2 (04_kings.tex line 93) says that in the promotion game a certificate makes a Z-move a loss, "so (V3) holds". (V3) is defined at line 60 as a statement "in chess", and the paper itself shows two lines later that Kb4-c5 has a horizon-1 certificate yet draws in chess. So the inference is wrong as written. The conclusion (line 23) already says the theorem "settles the promotion game but not chess", so the author's intent is clear and the damage is limited to this sentence and the Introduction's wording. It is a genuine wording fix, but less than major. The Introduction (line 38) only says "conditions (V1)--(V3)" and does not itself claim that a certificate suffices. A referee would still flag line 93.
verdict.better_fix: Replace the second half of the sentence in Theorem 4.2 with: "so the promotion-game analogue of (V3) holds wherever every move in $Z$ has one; for chess, (V3) needs the further check that a won promotion race is a won game (next paragraph)." Severity is moderate, not major.

confirmed.quote: with all other pawns removed, the punisher promotes within $h$ moves of its reply even if the defender may pass at any time, the defender cannot promote anywhere within $h$ moves
confirmed.problem: The certificate is not precisely defined. (a) If all other pawns are removed, the 'counter-promotion condition' cannot mention context pawns, yet Theorem 4.3 and Proposition 4.5 (and Conjecture 4.6) are about 'every chess-legal context', and the Conjecture says the condition fails in some context. Read literally, the theorem would hold with other pawns present only if the defender's context pawns are also counted; the text does not say so. (b) The tempo count is undefined: whether the reply is the first of the h moves, who moves first after it, and the tie rule decide whether 'cannot be weakened to h-1' is true. (c) Which of the defender's pawns count (Z-pawns versus context pawns) is not stated.
confirmed.fix: State the three parts separately: '(i) local forcing: with the other pawns removed, after the reply the punisher promotes by force within h of its own moves against a defender who may pass; (ii) counter-promotion: no pawn of the defender, in Z or in the context, can promote within h of its own moves after the reply, and the defender moves first after the reply; (iii) the defender is never stalemated on the forcing line.' Then say that Theorem 4.3 holds for contexts satisfying (ii).

verdict.reason: The certificate definition at 04_kings.tex lines 87-89 is ambiguous in a way that affects correctness. "With all other pawns removed" can only scope the forcing clause. If it also scoped the counter-promotion clause, that condition would not depend on context pawns. Yet Proposition 4.5 (line 107) states the counter-promotion condition "holds in every chess-legal context", and Conjecture 4.6 says some context leaves a move unpunished. So the condition must count context pawns. Theorem 4.3 is stated for the promotion game in the actual position. If a context pawn of the defender could promote within h moves, the theorem would fail, so the theorem needs the counter-promotion clause to cover context pawns as well. Nothing in the text says this. The other points also hold. The tempo count is undefined: whether the reply is the first of the h moves and who moves next. This matters for the claim that the condition "cannot be weakened to h-1", and for the example with horizon 1 that ends in a draw (lines 96-99). Which defender pawns count is not stated either. The severity is perhaps moderate rather than major, because a reader can infer the intent from Proposition 4.5.
verdict.better_fix: Replace lines 87-89 with a three-part definition. A move in Z has a certificate of horizon h if (i) local forcing: with all pawns outside Z removed, after the reply the punisher promotes within h of its own moves against a defender who may pass at any time; (ii) counter-promotion: after the reply, with the defender to move, no pawn of the defender, in Z or in the context, can promote within h of its own moves; (iii) the defender is never stalemated on the forcing line. State explicitly that Theorem 4.3 and Proposition 4.5 refer to clause (ii) evaluated in the full position, and that "cannot be weakened to h-1" means the same clause with h-1 in place of h.

confirmed.quote: We write $S(X)$ for the sum model of a pawn position $X$ and $W(X)$ for the whole-board game, which ends at the first passed pawn.
confirmed.problem: S(X) is never defined. Proposition 5.4 and Theorem 5.3 only make sense if the position is re-split into components along empty files at every node (a single-component X has S(X) equal to W(X) with a static decomposition, yet Proposition 5.4 says S(X) differs). Theorem 5.3's proof also needs the value of a component that has just acquired a passed pawn (+B, -B, or by the race rule) and the fact that a move is a move in one component. None of this is stated.
confirmed.fix: Add: 'S(X) is the game in which, at every position, the pawns are split into components along empty files (a ring if no file is empty), a component containing a passed pawn is replaced by the number +B or -B (by the race rule if both sides have one), and a move is a move in one component; the outcome is that of the resulting sum of games and numbers.'

verdict.reason: The finding overstates the gap but the core is valid. S(X) is not "never defined": Section 2 (02_rules.tex, Components) defines components along empty files and rings. Section 5 line 90 says a component with a passed pawn "becomes ±BIG". Section 5's "Two models" paragraph and Section 8 mention "splitting". What is missing is one place that says S(X) re-splits the position into components after every move, and that a component with a passed pawn is replaced by the number ±BIG. Without this, Proposition 5.4 reads as a contradiction. X is "a single component", yet S(X) differs from W(X), and that only holds if S(X) re-splits after captures (or after pawns are lost), which is stated only indirectly in Section 8 ("captures can split the ring"). Theorem 5.3's hypotheses ("two or more components", HSS) also presuppose the dynamic decomposition. A one-sentence definition would remove the ambiguity, but this is a clarity fix, not a correctness error, so it is moderate rather than major.
verdict.better_fix: In 05_sums.tex after line 92, replace "We write $S(X)$ for the sum model of a pawn position $X$" with: "We write $S(X)$ for the sum model of a pawn position $X$: after every move the pawns are re-split into components along empty files (one ring if no file is empty); a component in which a side has a passed pawn is replaced by the number $+\BIG$ or $-\BIG$ (by the race rule if both sides have one); a move is a move in one component; and the outcome is that of the resulting sum of games and numbers." Optionally add "(so a single component can split after a capture)" to link to Proposition 5.4. The values $\pm\BIG$ already appear in the preceding sentence.

Here the same pattern is counted as a mutual zugzwang. The following sentence then applies the term to the trebuchet of Fig. 4a, which is a mutual zugzwang in the first sense and is not a KPK position.
confirmed.fix: Define the KPK notion separately, e.g. 'reciprocal zugzwangs (white to move draws, black to move loses)', use that term in the text and in the column header of Table 11, and keep 'mutual zugzwang' for positions where the side to move loses whichever side it is. Edit the sentence on the trebuchet of Fig. 4a accordingly.

verdict.reason: The inconsistency is real. 10_tablebases.tex line 112 and the Table 11 header count "mutual zugzwangs" as KPK positions where white to move draws and black to move loses. 05_sums.tex (lines 56 and 75-78) calls exactly that pattern, the 7.2 king group, "not mutual" and "a zugzwang for black only". verdict.better_fix: Use "reciprocal zugzwang" for the KPK pattern (white to move draws, black to move loses). Change line 112, the Table 11 caption and column header, and the "share of ... zugzwangs" sentence on line 136 to match. State once which sense applies to "Ka3, Pa2 against Ka5" at line 139. Keep "mutual zugzwang" only for positions where the side to move loses whichever side it is, such as the trebuchet of Fig. 4a. confirmed.quote: Replace every end position not known to be $\pm\BIG$ by $-2\BIG$, or by $+2\BIG$
confirmed.problem: 'Known to be +-B' is ambiguous. End positions known to be 0, {B|-B} or a draw switch are not '+-B' but are known exactly, and replacing them by -2B/+2B is looser than intended. The bounds O^- and O^+ are valid either way, but the certificate 'if O^- = O^+' would then almost never hold for trees with hot or zero leaves, contradicting how it is used for 1/8.
confirmed.fix: Write: 'Replace every end position whose real-chess value is not known by -2B (for O^-) or +2B (for O^+), and keep every known leaf (+B, -B, 0, {B|-B}, or a draw switch).' Keep the monotonicity argument: raising any option, Left or Right, never lowers a game.

verdict.reason: At 09_real.tex:18 the Sandwich Lemma says to replace "every end position not known to be $\pm\BIG$". Definition def:oracle gives the end-position values as +B, -B, {B|-B}, 0 or {B r_W | B r_B}. Read literally, "not known to be ±B" covers the known leaves {B|-B}, 0 and the draw switches as well as the unresolved ones. The bounds still hold, since every leaf lies in [-2B, 2B]. But the certificate "if O^- = O^+" would then rarely fire, because a hot or zero leaf replaced by -2B and by +2B pulls the two values apart. Prop. eighth-real and the later text on "end positions still open" show the intended meaning is that only unresolved leaves are replaced. The nearby words "the unknown results" point the same way, but the lemma's own quantifier is ambiguous on the one point the certificate depends on. This is a small clarity fix, not an error in the mathematics.
verdict.better_fix: Write: "Replace every end position whose real-chess value is not known by $-2\BIG$ (for $O^-$) or by $+2\BIG$ (for $O^+$), and keep every known end position ($+\BIG$, $-\BIG$, $\game{+\BIG}{-\BIG}$, $0$, or a draw switch)."

confirmed.quote: the cylinder has fewer legal positions, since the kings
confirmed.problem: The reason given is incomplete. Black-to-move legal counts fall by 168,024 - 165,984 = 2,040, which is the king-adjacency effect. White-to-move counts fall by 163,328 - 160,656 = 2,672, which is more. A white pawn on the a- or h-file now also attacks across the seam, so the black king may not stand there when white is to move. T44 (research/kpkp/t44/REPORT.md) names both causes for KPKP.
confirmed.fix: Replace 'since the kings may not touch across the seam' with 'since the kings may not touch across the seam and, with white to move, the black king may not stand on a square a white pawn attacks across the seam'.

verdict.reason: The sentence at line 74 reads "the cylinder has fewer legal positions, since the kings may not touch across the seam", and that is incomplete. Table kpk gives White-to-move drops of 163,328 to 160,656 (2,672) and Black-to-move drops of 168,024 to 165,984 (2,040). KPK has only a white pawn, so Black-to-move positions lose only king-adjacency cases. With White to move, the cylinder adds a second exclusion: the black king cannot stand on a square the white pawn attacks across the seam, because that would leave the black king in check on White's turn. That explains why the White-to-move drop is larger. The paper never mentions this effect for KPK. The author's own T44 report (kpkp/t44) lists "king adjacency or pawn attack across the seam" as the cause of the flat-legal positions with no cylinder twin. The inconsistency is minor but real, and a referee could check it against the table.
verdict.better_fix: Replace "since the kings may not touch across the seam" with "since the kings may not touch across the seam and, with white to move, the black king may not stand on a square that the white pawn attacks across the seam".

confirmed.quote: with frozen kings and queen promotions only, the one-eighth survives in real chess
confirmed.problem: "Frozen kings" and "real chess" contradict each other. The 1/8 is the value of a pawn tree whose leaves come from tablebases and the authors' solver. The kings are assumed to be frozen at every internal node. Section 4 says this assumption fails: 41 of 449 king moves beside T draw and 7 win (04_kings l.161-163). It also says the zero is trusted only beside slow or locked components (l.122). Section 9 titles the result "Towards a real-chess 1/8" and 09_real l.68 says the 1/8 "assumes the frozen kings". The Proposition (09_real l.63) is nonetheless named "A real-chess 1/8". The Introduction (l.49-51) and Conclusion repeat the claim. The labelled result is a model-with-chess-leaves value; it is not a value of a chess position.
confirmed.fix: Abstract: "with the kings frozen inside the tree and queen promotions only, a hybrid oracle value built from tablebase results at the leaves equals 1/8; whether the actual 10-man position has value 1/8 is open." Rename the Proposition "A tablebase-backed oracle value of 1/8" and drop "survives in real chess" from the abstract, Introduction and Conclusion.

verdict.reason: The wording problem is real, though less severe than "major" or "contradiction". The abstract does state the qualifiers "frozen kings and queen promotions only". But 09_real.tex l.68 says "This $1/8$ assumes the frozen kings of the tree". The title "Towards a real-chess 1/8" fits that. 04_kings.tex l.161-163 says the convention calls all 449 king moves beside a trebuchet losing, yet 41 draw and 7 win. l.122 says the zero is trusted only beside slow or locked components. So the value is a hybrid: tablebase and solver leaves under a frozen-kings tree. The abstract sentence "the one-eighth survives in real chess" and the Proposition title "A real-chess 1/8" (09_real.tex l.63) are unqualified in the headline places. They read as a claim about the actual chess position, which the paper itself says is open. The Introduction (01_intro.tex ~l.49-51) is more careful ("oracle value ... is exactly 1/8"), so the overclaim is mainly in the abstract, the Proposition title and the Conclusion (14_conclusion.tex l.7).
verdict.better_fix: Abstract: replace "with frozen kings and queen promotions only, the one-eighth survives in real chess" with "with the kings frozen inside the pawn tree and queen promotions only, the oracle value, which takes its leaves from tablebases and our solver, is exactly one-eighth; whether the full-chess position has this value is open." Rename the Proposition "A tablebase-backed oracle value of 1/8". Make the same change at 14_conclusion.tex l.7. Leave the Introduction as it is, since it already says "oracle value".

confirmed.quote: but star two appears with seven, in one position and its color-reversed twin, confirmed by three programs
confirmed.problem: The headline result (an answer to the *2 question) omits three qualifiers. (i) Positions A and B are values of the sum/whole-board pawn model, not of chess. Their real-chess oracle values are open, and the 9- to 11-man end positions are unsolved (09_real l.70-74; 14_conclusion item 2). (ii) "Seven pawns" excludes the two pawns of T, so the position has 9 pawns and 11 men, which matters when comparing with Drummond-Cole's and Elkies' piece counts. (iii) The pawn-history legality of A and B rests on "we checked these histories by hand" (08_star2 l.69), with no proof game given. The closing sentence of 08_star2 l.183 says the question "has a positive answer on the ordinary 8x8 board". Yet the paper's own textbook *2 candidate failed this same transfer to real chess.
confirmed.fix: Abstract: "In the pawn model with frozen kings (a trebuchet adds two pawns, 11 men in all), *2 appears with seven pawns, in one position and its color-reversed twin; its real-chess status is open." Add proof games for A and B, or an appendix move list, so the legality claim can be checked.

verdict.reason: The core point holds, but it is smaller than "major". The abstract sets up the frozen-kings, passed-pawn-wins model in its first sentences, so "star two appears with seven" is arguably in-model. Even so, the abstract never says the real-chess status of *2 is open. Its next sentence says "the one-eighth survives in real chess", which invites a reader to assume the *2 result transfers too. 09_real.tex l.70-74 says the oracle values of A and B are open: the 9- to 11-man end positions are unsolved, so their *2 is a model value. 08_star2.tex l.183 says the question "has a positive answer" "in the model", which is correctly hedged. The abstract should carry the same hedge. The legality claim ("we checked these histories by hand", 08_star2 l.69) names the captures c2xd3 and b7xa6 but gives no proof game. A move list would let a reader check it. The piece-count point is mostly handled: the body says "Positions A and B have 11 men beside T", but the abstract's "seven" counts only the pawns not belonging to T. The other referee's remark that the paper's own textbook *2 candidate failed the transfer to real chess is not something I checked.
verdict.better_fix: Abstract: "...*2 appears in the pawn model with seven pawns beside T (11 men in all), in one position and its color-reversed twin, confirmed by three programs; its real-chess value is open." Also add proof games for A and B in an appendix, or at least the capture sequences, in place of "we checked these histories by hand". Treat as moderate severity.

confirmed.quote: A position with a pawn on every file, a \emph{ring}, has no edge at which to cut
confirmed.problem: A ring uses every file. A king group needs a buffer of neighboring files holding no pawns (04_kings l.50-51), and Theorem 4 needs a king group Z. So no ring component can sit beside a frozen king group, and all cylinder-only and ring results are pure pawn-model statements: the abstract's "three-file cylinder six pawns", "ten files ... one pawn per file" and "seven files ten-pawn rings reach star three", and Proposition 6.1. They are not cylinder-chess endgame values. The paper never says this, although RESULTS.md notes it (0 of 40 placements can be frozen on the 8-file cylinder). The title and framing ("chess endgames on a cylindrical chessboard") suggest otherwise, and the significance of the ring results for chess is not explained.
confirmed.fix: Add to Section 6 and to the Introduction: "A ring leaves no empty file for a trebuchet and its buffer, so ring values are values of the pawn model; with kings on the board the frozen-king convention cannot be applied to them and their chess meaning is unknown." Qualify the abstract sentence accordingly, e.g. "in the pawn-only model".

verdict.reason: The logic holds. 04_kings.tex l.50-51 defines a king group Z with a buffer of pawn-free neighboring files, and Theorem 4 (validity) needs such a Z. A ring has a pawn on every file (02_rules.tex l.112), so no buffer can exist beside it and the frozen-king convention cannot apply to any position containing a ring. RESULTS.md l.31 notes the related failure on the 8-file cylinder (0 of 40 placements can be frozen). The paper never says this. 01_intro l.17 and 02_rules l.124 call rings the source of cylinder-only values. 08_star2 l.3-4 asks about "a king-and-pawn position". confirmed.quote: \emph{count}: fewer moves to promote wins; the side that did not move goes first and wins a tie;
confirmed.problem: The race rule is one of the three parameters that define the nine settings and it changes values (3/4 becomes 0 under the mover rule; 06_atlas l.61). It is not defined precisely. "Moves to promote" is not specified: does it count the double step, ignore blockers and captures, use the fastest passed pawn or all of them, and how are non-passed pawns treated? Theorem 7.1 then asserts the 1/8 for "every assignment of outcomes to its race positions", and the term "race positions" is never defined. The sum model (BIG=256) and the whole-board model are also never given a formal definition of end of game. A reader cannot reimplement the model from the text.
confirmed.fix: Add a definition: "For each side, let d be the minimum over its passed pawns of the number of moves to reach the last rank on an empty file, counting a double step as one move from the starting rank; the side with smaller d wins, and if d is equal the side that did not just move wins." Define "race position" in Section 2.

verdict.reason: Confirmed in 02_rules.tex l.37-41. The count rule reads only "fewer moves to promote wins; the side that did not move goes first and wins a tie". The paper never says whether the double step counts, whether blockers or captures on the way are ignored, or which pawns count. The count rule is one of three parameters behind the nine settings, and 06_atlas.tex l.61 says it changes values (3/4 becomes 0 under the mover rule). Theorem 7.1 (07_targets.tex l.58) quantifies over "every assignment of outcomes to its race positions", and "race position" is not defined anywhere in the sections (grep finds only that one use). The tie wording is also loose: "the side that did not move goes first" could be read two ways. The finding is somewhat overstated. Theorem 7.1's statement is intuitive enough, since a race position is one where both sides have a passed pawn. The sum and whole-board models are defined by the normal-play rules in 02_rules.tex and the ±BIG convention, so the "never given a formal definition of end of game" claim is weak. The core complaint stands: a reader cannot reimplement the count rule from the text.
verdict.better_fix: Narrow the fix to the count rule and the term "race position". In 02_rules.tex after l.41, add: "A race position is one in which both sides have a passed pawn after a move. For each side, d is the least number of moves any of its passed pawns needs to reach the last rank, ignoring all other pieces, with a double step from the starting rank counted as one move. The smaller d wins. On equal d, the side to move next (the side that did not make the last move) wins." The author should check this against the code (the solver's race-rule function) before using it, because the exact convention, including whether the counting is over passed pawns only and the tie handling, must match the programs. Then change Theorem 7.1 to "...for every assignment of outcomes to its race positions (Section 2.1)".

confirmed.quote:
but infinitesimals only $30\%$ ($26\%$ at depth~2) and nimbers $53\%$
\lab{C1}: exactly the tempo and parity fights that CGT singles out.
confirmed.problem: The causal reading (CGT class explains engine error) is not supported. The sample is small: 17 nimbers and 27 infinitesimals. No control for confounds (men count, locked-pawn structure, distance to the decisive capture) is reported. The class "number" never reaches 100% (98% at depth 12), so the claim that classes separate is only partly visible in Table 5. The Introduction (01_intro l.56) states "Stockfish is weakest on infinitesimals at low depth" as a finding without the "pilot" caveat given in the body (l.20). Section 12.4 concedes that errors on sums "do not single out nimbers or infinitesimals". The engines section also has no stated relation to the CGT results of the other sections, so its significance is unexplained.
confirmed.fix: Report confidence intervals or a test (e.g. Fisher exact for infinitesimal vs rest at depth 1). Restate the Introduction bullet as "in a pilot of 233 positions, Stockfish at depth 1 scored lowest on infinitesimals (8 of 27 vs 73-81% elsewhere); no effect was seen on sums". Add a sentence on why this matters for CGT, or move the section to a short remark.

verdict.reason:
The finding is real but much narrower than stated. Most of it is a misreading or already handled in the paper. The remaining defect is a modest overclaim.

Not valid:
- The section already says "With one engine and a small sample, this is a pilot result" (12_engines.tex, l.20).
- Section 12.4 openly states that errors on sums "do not single out nimbers or infinitesimals".
- The remark that the "number" class never reaches 100% (98% at depth 12) is irrelevant, because the paper does not claim every class reaches 100%.
- The sample sizes (n=17 and n=27) are printed in Table 5.
- The tablebase disagreement on 52 positions is disclosed.

Valid:
1. 12_engines.tex l.18 says "exactly the tempo and parity fights that CGT singles out". That is a causal explanation for a pattern the data only weakly support. With n=17 nimbers and n=27 infinitesimals there is no test or confidence interval. The "other" class (60% at depth 1, 50% at depth 2) is nearly as low as nimbers (53%), and "other" has no tempo or parity interpretation. The size of the infinitesimal gap (8 of 27, 30%, against 73-81% elsewhere) probably is significant, but the nimber gap is not clearly distinguishable from "other".
2. 01_intro.tex l.56 states "Stockfish is weakest on infinitesimals at low depth" without the pilot qualifier given in the body.

Suggested fix:
- In 12_engines.tex, replace "\lab{C1}: exactly the tempo and parity fights that CGT singles out." with "\lab{C1}, consistent with, though not shown to be caused by, tempo and parity fights; the nimber and 'other' classes are not clearly separated at this sample size."
- In the introduction, write "in a $233$-position pilot, Stockfish at low depth is weakest on infinitesimals".
- Optionally add a Fisher exact p-value for infinitesimal against the rest at depth 1.

Severity is minor, as the original referee said.
verdict.better_fix: Replace "exactly the tempo and parity fights that CGT singles out" with "consistent with tempo and parity fights, though the nimber and 'other' classes are not clearly separated at this sample size". Add "in a 233-position pilot" to the Introduction bullet (01_intro.tex l.56). Optionally add a Fisher exact test for infinitesimal vs rest at depth 1.

rejected.problem: The default race rule is not reproducible from the text. The implementation (cylcgt/pawns.py, promote_distance) counts a pawn on its starting rank as one move closer (double step), counts only the front pawn of each file, and ignores e.p.-capturable pawns. These choices change values. I re-solved Proposition 5.4 (X = W b2 d4 g3 h5 / B a7 c7 f7 g4 on C8, e.p. off) with a plain 'ranks to go' count and got a black win for both W(X) and S(X) (no first-player win in W(X)). With the double-step-aware count I get the paper's result (W(X) first-player win, S(X) black win). So the paper's stated rule gives a different answer from the one it reports on a headline example.
rejected.why_rejected: The rule is "fewer moves to promote". Under the rules of chess, a pawn on its starting rank can promote in one move fewer, because the double step is a single move. promote_distance in cylcgt/pawns.py (line 48) implements exactly that, so the code matches the literal reading of the text. The referee's "plain ranks to go" count is a non-literal reading, and the discrepancy comes from that reading. The other two objections do not hold. First, "front pawn only" cannot change the minimum. A friendly pawn ahead on the same file is always nearer to promotion than the pawn behind it, so counting the blocked pawn adds nothing. Second, the e.p.-capturable exclusion is already stated in Section 2.3 and enforced by the PASSED_RESPECTS_EP flag, which the paper's e.p.-aware passed test (Section 2.3) covers. That leaves only a clarity issue: a short parenthetical such as "(a double step counts as one move)" would help, but it is not a correctness problem.

rejected.problem: Stated unconditionally, this is false in the paper's own model. With en passant a right created in one component survives moves in another, so the whole board is not the sum (Proposition 5.5 gives a pure pawn position where the sum has the wrong outcome). With the passed-pawn convention the whole board ends at the first passed pawn while the sum does not (Section 5.3, Proposition 5.4).
rejected.why_rejected: The sentence at 02_rules.tex line 110-111 states the file-independence decomposition. Section II also ends with "Section~\ref{sec:sums-hss} says when a sum of components still names the right winner". Section 5.3 (05_sums.tex, "When Is the Sum Model Right?") opens by separating the sum model S(X) from the whole-board game W(X), and its theorem excludes pending en passant (condition E). So the paper does not claim that the sum equals the whole board. The only issue is that the rules sentence is looser than the later qualification, which is a matter of wording and not an error a referee would require fixed.

The paper defines no extra-option games as nimbers, and the "no position is *k" claims are about game values, which are equal up to canonical form. The suggested rewording is harmless but a matter of taste, not a correctness or clarity defect.

rejected.problem: The sketch skips the cases that make HSS the right hypothesis. (i) The passed pawn can be created by black's move or by white's, and HSS must count threats created by either side's move (the Definition does, but the sketch does not use it). (ii) The component that has just received the passed pawn can itself split or carry a black threat; after it becomes +B, the sum model stops play there, so it needs the statement that no later position of that component gives black a passed pawn. (iii) A move giving both sides passed pawns in one component needs the race rule. As written the sketch does not show where each hypothesis, including B > number of moves, enters.
rejected.why_rejected: This is a complaint that a proof sketch is short, and the paper already handles it. The theorem is labelled [S], so it is a sketch with the full induction in the repository. Definition `def:hss` already counts threats from "moves of either side, in any order", so point (i) is covered by the definition. The theorem statement carries the "BIG exceeds the number of moves" hypothesis, and the sketch's phrase "black runs out of moves before white's +BIG does" is where it is used. Point (ii) is a detail of the induction that the sketch defers to the repository, and the sketch says so. The proposed replacement also adds an unproved "monotonicity" step and mentions a "race rule" that the theorem does not define. It is a matter of exposition taste, not a correctness error.

rejected.problem: Both halves overclaim relative to Section 4. The e.p.-aware test addresses only 18 of the 159 convention failures (04_kings l.157-160). In 13 of those 18 the free kings change the result again, so the count falls only "from 143 to 138". On the paper's own sample, the convention is still wrong in roughly 138 of 500 cases (the whole-sample figure under the new test is never stated; the ambiguous "there" refers to the seven-file cylinder). "Say when the frozen kings are exact" rests on Theorem 4 [S]. Its hypotheses (V2),(V3) are statements about chess that restate the conclusion. Conjecture 1 says no context-free local test exists for h>=2, and real trebuchets need h of about 5-7. So no general criterion is actually given.
rejected.why_rejected: The body of the paper already reports what the finding says is missing. Section 4 (04_kings.tex l.157-160) gives the figures: 159 of 500 convention failures, 107 through the kings alone, 18 through en passant, and 13 of those 18 changing again with free kings, so the count falls only from 143 to 138. Section 4.2 is titled "When Is the Frozen Trébuchet Exact?". It states the conditions (V1)-(V4) and the horizon-h certificate, and it says openly where each fails: Conjecture 1 is tagged Conj, the local test for (V2) is only [S], and l.84-85 describes kings walking to the pawns. So "say when the frozen kings are exact" is a fair one-line summary of sufficient conditions. The abstract is also length-limited. The one fair point is that the whole-sample residual under the new test is not stated; the paper gives it only for the seven-file cylinder. The sentence "We repair this model" is slightly generous but not misleading, since the paper itself says the repair is partial. This is wording at most, not a correctness problem.

rejected.problem: The theorem's content is thin and its label inconsistent. (V2) ("the side that gets a passed pawn wins") and (V3) ("every move in Z loses") are statements about chess outcomes that are the conclusion in disguise. The three-line "proof sketch" is the entire proof, so [S] ("independent check pending") understates it, and the result is closer to a definition. (V1) mixes "legal chess moves are exactly the moves of the model" with "the side to move has a legal move", while the proof uses "has a model move". These are different when the only legal move is a king move in Z. The substantive results are the local tests (Theorem 4.3, Proposition 4.4). They cover only the promotion game, not chess; Conjecture 1 says they cannot extend. So the Introduction's claim that (V1)-(V3) give "the result of the whole-board pawn game" is vacuous unless (V2),(V3) can be verified. The only verification offered is brute force on a 500-component sweep, which then fails in 27%.
rejected.why_rejected: This is mostly taste or a misreading. (1) The [S] label is conservative, not an overclaim. Marking a short argument "sketch, independent check pending" understates rather than overstates it, so no referee would object on correctness grounds. (2) The V1 mismatch is not real. V1 says legal chess moves are exactly the model's moves, so "has a legal move" and "has a model move" are the same thing. The model includes moves in Z, and a lone legal Z move is itself a decisive event. By V3 that move loses, so the proof at lines 67-69 handles it. (3) The claim that V2 and V3 are the conclusion in disguise is overstated. They are explicit hypotheses, and the paper says so. Lines 83-85 list how each can fail, and lines 87-110 give local tests (the horizon-h certificate, the passed-pawn condition) and counterexamples. Calling the theorem a reduction lemma with stated hypotheses is accurate. (4) The point about "beside T" scope in Sections 7-8 is a fair request for clarity but not a defect in this theorem. The finding does not show the Introduction's wording is wrong, and the paper already states the conditions can fail. At most this is an optional clarity improvement, not a problem the author must fix.
